extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners of scientific method, induction, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains the canonical experimental/inductive methods (Agreement, Difference, Joint/Indirect Difference, Residues, Concomitant Variations) used to infer causal relations from observations and experiments. Emphasizes their canons, applications, limitations, and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare instances in which the phenomenon occurs and identify the antecedent circumstance common to them as connected with the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicable especially where artificial experimentation is impossible and often the only directly inductive resource. Use by comparing all known substances/instances that exhibit the phenomenon and finding a common circumstance (example: doubly refracting substances are crystalline). Limitation: the converse need not hold (common antecedent may not be sufficient), and the method can be imperfect because instances may agree in more than one antecedent; hence it gives evidence of connection but not necessarily direct causation without further tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare instances that are identical except for the presence/absence of a single antecedent to determine whether that antecedent is the cause (or part of the cause) of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More efficacious where we can produce phenomena at pleasure (artificial experimentation). This method can ascertain causes as well as mere laws by finding positive and negative instances differing only in the antecedent A. Requires ability to isolate and vary antecedents; when that is impossible (e.g., composite antecedents that cannot be separated), the direct Method of Difference cannot be used. The Method of Residues is a modification of this method (see Residues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Method of Difference / Joint Method of Agreement and Difference (Third Canon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use two independent applications of the Method of Agreement — one among instances where the phenomenon occurs, the other among instances where it does not — and identify the circumstance in which the two sets differ as the cause or indispensable part of the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canon (Third Canon): "If two or more instances in which the phenomenon occurs have only one circumstance in common, while two or more instances in which it does not occur have nothing in common save the absence of that circumstance, the circumstance in which alone the two sets of instances differ, is the effect, or the cause, or an indispensable part of the cause, of the phenomenon." Use when the direct Method of Difference is unavailable because antecedents cannot be separated. Each of the two agreement proofs should be independent and corroborative. Limitation: not equivalent in cogency to direct Method of Difference because one cannot be sure that the agreeing instances differ in nothing else besides A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues (Fourth Canon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtract from a complex phenomenon those parts already ascribed to known antecedents by previous inductions; the remainder (residue) is the effect of the remaining antecedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canon (Fourth Canon): "Subduct from any phenomenon such part as is known by previous inductions to be the effect of certain antecedents, and the residue of the phenomenon is the effect of the remaining antecedents." This is a peculiar modification of the Method of Difference: the negative instance is arrived at deductively rather than observed directly. It is rigorous provided the earlier inductions were obtained by infallible methods and one is certain that the residual antecedent is the only one unaccounted for. Practical guidance: where possible, obtain the residual antecedent artificially and test it separately, or account for its agency deductively. Strengths: fertile in discovering obscure agents or effects that would not present themselves otherwise. Limitations: uncertain unless the uniqueness of the residual antecedent can be established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations (Fifth Canon)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one phenomenon varies in any manner whenever another phenomenon varies in some particular manner, then it is either a cause or an effect of that phenomenon, or connected with it by causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canon (Fifth Canon): "Whatever phenomenon varies in any manner whenever another phenomenon varies in some particular manner, is either a cause or an effect of that phenomenon, or is connected with it through some fact of causation." Useful when antecedents cannot be wholly excluded but can be modified (quantity or relation). Use to infer causal connection from systematic co-variation (examples: heat and expansion, lunar position and tides, amount of obstacles and retardation of motion). Precautions: concomitance alone cannot distinguish direct causation from common-cause relations; one should attempt to produce the variations experimentally or otherwise use the Method of Difference to hold other antecedents constant. Requires knowledge of absolute quantities when inferring numerical laws and caution when extrapolating beyond observed limits (risk of hidden counteracting causes or incorrect numerical law). Where A varies in quantity and a varies proportionally, one may infer proportional causal influence, but only within the observed limits and with awareness of possible other contributing causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precautions and limits common to the four methods
rubrics_metrics.description: General rules for valid application: retain other antecedents unchanged when testing one antecedent; ensure instances compared differ only as required; be cautious about extrapolation beyond observed ranges; where possible, try decisive experiments or obtain independent corroboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Across all methods one must attempt to hold other antecedents constant (or account for them), be aware that agreement does not prove sufficiency, and recognize the possibility of hidden or counteracting causes. Numerical inferences require knowledge of absolute quantities. The methods together, with deduction, compose the available resources for ascertaining laws by specific observation and experiment; but each method has characteristic uncertainties which must be guarded against (e.g., inability to isolate permanent causes, limits of observed variation, and potential dormant agents beyond observation).
